We get asymptotics for the volume of large balls in an arbitrary locally compact group G with polynomial growth. This is done via a study of the geometry of G and a generalization of P. Pansu's thesis. In particular, we show that any such G is weakly commensurable to some simply connected solvable Lie group S, the Lie shadow of G. We also show that large balls in G have an asymptotic shape, i.e. after a suitable renormalization, they converge to a limiting compact set which can be interpreted geometrically. We then discuss the speed of convergence, treat some examples and give an application to ergodic theory. We also answer a question of Burago about left invariant metrics and recover some results of Stoll on the irrationality of growth series of nilpotent groups.

# Asymptotic Geometry of Groups with Polynomial Growth

This paper presents a comprehensive study of the geometric structure underlying locally compact groups exhibiting polynomial growth, establishing several fundamental results that extend and generalize the foundational work of P. Pansu.

## Main Results and Methodology

The central contribution of the paper is the derivation of precise asymptotic formulas describing the volume growth of large balls in any locally compact group $G$ with polynomial growth. This is achieved through a careful analysis of the geometric structure of $G$, combined with a substantial generalization of the techniques originally developed in Pansu's thesis. Whereas Pansu's approach was tailored to specific settings, the methods introduced here extend the analysis to the broader and more general context of arbitrary locally compact groups satisfying the polynomial growth condition.

## The Lie Shadow Construction

A key structural result established in the paper is that every locally compact group $G$ of polynomial growth is weakly commensurable to a simply connected solvable Lie group $S$. This group $S$, which the authors term the **Lie shadow** of $G$, serves as a canonical geometric model that captures the essential large-scale structure of $G$. The existence of this Lie shadow provides a powerful bridge between the potentially complicated structure of a general locally compact group and the more tractable, well-understood theory of solvable Lie groups, allowing many questions about $G$ to be translated into questions about $S$.

## Asymptotic Shape of Balls

Building on this correspondence, the authors demonstrate that large balls in $G$ possess a well-defined **asymptotic shape**. More precisely, they show that after suitable renormalization, the sequence of balls of increasing radius converges to a limiting compact set. This limiting object is not merely an abstract construction but admits a concrete geometric interpretation, tying the analytic behavior of ball volumes to an underlying geometric structure that reflects the large-scale properties of the group. This result significantly refines earlier growth estimates by providing not just asymptotic volume formulas but a genuine shape-theoretic description of how balls behave as their radius tends to infinity.

## Rate of Convergence and Applications

The paper further investigates the **rate of convergence** toward this asymptotic shape, providing quantitative estimates that complement the qualitative existence result. To illustrate the theory, the authors present a collection of instructive examples that clarify how the abstract machinery applies in concrete settings. Additionally, the paper includes an application to **ergodic theory**, demonstrating the broader relevance of these geometric results beyond the immediate context of growth theory.

## Resolution of Open Problems and Recovery of Prior Results

The paper's contributions extend to resolving a previously open question posed by **Burago** concerning left invariant metrics on groups of polynomial growth. In addition, the results obtained here allow the authors to recover earlier findings due to **Stoll** on the irrationality of growth series for nilpotent groups, situating these prior results within the more general and unified framework developed in this work. This demonstrates the wide-reaching scope of the paper's methods, which not only establish new results but also provide fresh, more conceptual proofs of previously known theorems.

# On the Asymptotic Geometry of Groups with Polynomial Growth

## Introduction

The study of groups with polynomial volume growth has a rich history, beginning with the foundational work of Gromov, who characterized such groups (among finitely generated groups) as being virtually nilpotent. This structural result opened the door to a finer analysis of the *geometric* asymptotics of these groups—not merely their algebraic classification, but the precise shape of their balls as they grow to infinity. Pansu's landmark 1983 thesis addressed this question for the case of nilpotent Lie groups equipped with left-invariant Riemannian (or more generally sub-Riemannian) metrics, showing that appropriately rescaled balls converge to balls of a homogeneous quasi-norm on the associated graded nilpotent Lie group. This paper extends and generalizes Pansu's asymptotic framework to the substantially broader setting of arbitrary locally compact groups with polynomial growth, equipped with a wide class of admissible metrics, including but not limited to word metrics arising from compact generating sets.

## The Lie Shadow Construction

Our first main contribution is structural: we show that every locally compact, compactly generated group $G$ with polynomial growth is *weakly commensurable* to a simply connected solvable Lie group, which we call the **Lie shadow** of $G$. Weak commensurability here refers to a relationship strictly weaker than the classical commensurability up to compact factors and finite-index subgroups; it allows for a more flexible correspondence that nonetheless preserves the essential coarse and asymptotic geometry of the group. 

The construction of the Lie shadow proceeds through a careful analysis of the structure theory of locally compact groups with polynomial growth, building on the structural results of Losert, Guivarc'h, and others concerning such groups. We show that the asymptotic cone of $G$—in the sense of Gromov-Hausdorff convergence of rescaled metric spaces—can always be realized as the asymptotic cone of its Lie shadow, a much more tractable simply connected solvable Lie group where explicit computations with one-parameter subgroups, exponential coordinates, and gradings become available. This reduction is essential: it transports questions about volume growth in general locally compact groups to questions that can be resolved using Lie-theoretic and representation-theoretic tools.

## Renormalized Convergence of Balls

The central geometric theorem of the paper establishes that, for any admissible left-invariant metric $d$ on $G$, the sequence of rescaled balls
$$
\frac{1}{n} B_d(n)
$$
converges, in the Gromov-Hausdorff (or Hausdorff, once embedded appropriately in the Lie shadow) sense, to a limiting compact convex set $K \subset \mathfrak{s}$, where $\mathfrak{s}$ denotes an appropriate graded vector space associated to the Lie algebra of the shadow. This limiting set $K$ admits an explicit geometric interpretation: it is the unit ball of a homogeneous quasi-norm constructed from the word metric's asymptotic behavior on the associated graded Lie algebra, generalizing Pansu's original limit shape but now accounting for the more intricate layering that arises from solvable (rather than purely nilpotent) structure.

As a direct consequence, we obtain sharp polynomial asymptotics
$$
\mathrm{vol}(B_d(n)) \sim C \, n^D
$$
where $D$ is computed explicitly in terms of the grading of the Lie shadow, and $C$ is expressed as the volume of the limiting shape $K$ with respect to a suitably normalized Haar measure. This refines earlier growth estimates, which typically only established polynomial growth up to bounded multiplicative constants, into a genuine asymptotic equivalence with an explicit and geometrically meaningful leading coefficient.

## Resolution of Burago's Question

A striking application of our main theorem is a complete resolution of a question posed by Burago concerning the comparison of left-invariant Riemannian (or Finsler) metrics on Lie groups with polynomial growth. Burago asked whether the volume growth function associated to any two left-invariant metrics on such a group must be asymptotically proportional, and moreover whether the ratio of volumes of large balls stabilizes. Using our renormalized convergence result, we show that this is indeed the case: for any two admissible left-invariant metrics $d_1$ and $d_2$ on $G$, the ratio
$$
\frac{\mathrm{vol}(B_{d_1}(n))}{\mathrm{vol}(B_{d_2}(n))}
$$
converges to an explicit constant determined by the ratio of volumes of the two corresponding limiting shapes $K_1$ and $K_2$ in the Lie shadow. This settles the question affirmatively in full generality, extending previously known partial results that were confined to nilpotent Lie groups or required additional symmetry assumptions.

## Recovering Stoll's Irrationality Results

Our framework also allows us to recover, via a unified and conceptual approach, the results of Stoll on the irrationality of growth series for certain nilpotent groups. Stoll had shown, through delicate combinatorial and number-theoretic arguments, that the growth series
$$
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |B(n)| \, t^n
$$
of certain nilpotent groups fails to be a rational function of $t$, in contrast to the behavior observed for many other classes of groups with polynomial growth (such as virtually abelian groups, where rationality is classical). We show that the precise asymptotic behavior of $\mathrm{vol}(B_d(n))$ dictated by our renormalization theorem—specifically, the presence of non-integer or incommensurable exponents and coefficients arising from the geometry of the limiting shape $K$—is fundamentally incompatible with the growth series being rational. This provides a conceptual, geometric explanation for Stoll's phenomenon, situating it within the broader asymptotic theory developed here, and suggests a general criterion for irrationality applicable beyond the specific examples originally considered by Stoll.

## Applications to Ergodic Theory

Finally, we describe applications of our results to ergodic theory, particularly in connection with the study of random walks and orbit equivalence on groups with polynomial growth. The precise volume asymptotics obtained here refine previously known bounds used in the study of return probabilities of random walks, allowing for sharper local limit theorems. Additionally, the explicit description of the limiting shape $K$ and its relationship to the Lie shadow's structure has implications for the study of boundary actions and the classification of invariant measures on horospherical-type foliations associated to the group's action on its asymptotic cone. We outline how these applications connect to existing work on the Choquet-Deny property and the Poisson boundary for groups of polynomial growth, indicating directions for further research where the geometric precision of our main theorem may yield new ergodic-theoretic invariants.

## Organization of the Paper

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we recall the necessary background on locally compact groups with polynomial growth and establish the existence and uniqueness (up to appropriate equivalence) of the Lie shadow. Section 3 develops the technical machinery for proving Gromov-Hausdorff convergence of rescaled balls, extending Pansu's original arguments to the solvable setting. Section 4 contains the proof of the main asymptotic volume theorem. Sections 5 and 6 are devoted to the applications: the resolution of Burago's question and the recovery of Stoll's irrationality results, respectively. We conclude in Section 7 with the ergodic-theoretic applications and a discussion of open questions suggested by this work.

# Pansu's Theorem and the Geometry of Lie Groups

The intersection of geometric analysis and Lie theory has produced some of the most elegant results in modern mathematics. Among these, the work of French mathematician Pierre Pansu stands out as a foundational contribution to our understanding of nilpotent Lie groups and their metric properties.

Pansu's most celebrated result, now known as **Pansu's Differentiability Theorem**, extends the classical Rademacher theorem to the setting of Carnot groups—a special class of stratified, nilpotent Lie groups equipped with a natural sub-Riemannian metric. This theorem establishes that Lipschitz maps between Carnot groups are almost everywhere differentiable, but with a crucial twist: the notion of "derivative" must be reinterpreted through the lens of the group's intrinsic dilation structure rather than the ordinary linear structure of Euclidean space.

This shift in perspective proved to be transformative. In classical analysis, differentiability is tied to linear approximation in vector spaces. Pansu showed that in the noncommutative, graded world of Carnot groups, the appropriate notion of derivative is a **homogeneous homomorphism**—a map compatible with the group's own dilations, which encode the anisotropic scaling inherent to these spaces. This insight opened new avenues for studying rigidity phenomena in geometric group theory, particularly in the classification of quasi-isometries between negatively curved spaces and their boundaries at infinity.

The relevance of Pansu's work extends deeply into the study of hyperbolic groups and symmetric spaces. Many boundaries of rank-one symmetric spaces, such as complex or quaternionic hyperbolic space, carry a natural Carnot group structure. Pansu's differentiability results became an essential tool in proving quasi-isometric rigidity theorems, showing that the large-scale geometry of certain Lie groups determines their algebraic structure up to natural equivalences.

More broadly, this line of research illustrates a recurring theme in modern geometry: the interplay between algebraic structure (the Lie group) and metric or analytic structure (differentiability, quasi-isometries). Pansu's contributions demonstrate that even highly abstract algebraic objects like nilpotent Lie groups possess rich geometric lives, governed by subtle analytic principles that generalize—rather than merely mimic—classical Euclidean intuition.

In this way, the legacy of Pansu's theorem continues to influence contemporary research at the crossroads of analysis, geometry, and group theory, serving as a bridge between the abstract world of Lie algebras and the concrete, measurable world of metric spaces.

# Abstract

We study the growth of balls in locally compact groups of polynomial growth, extending the seminal work of Gromov and Pansu on the structure of such groups. Let $G$ be a compactly generated locally compact group equipped with a word metric associated to a compact generating set, and suppose $G$ has polynomial growth of degree $d$. Building on Pansu's asymptotic cone construction, we establish precise estimates for the volume growth function $V(n) = |B(e,n)|$, refining the classical result $V(n) \asymp n^d$ to obtain sharp second-order asymptotics.

Our approach exploits the Lie-theoretic structure underlying groups of polynomial growth: by the Gromov–Losert theorem and its extensions, $G$ admits a compact normal subgroup $K$ such that $G/K$ is a Lie group, and the polycyclic/nilpotent structure of the associated graded Lie algebra governs the leading-order behavior of $V(n)$. We show that the rescaled balls $\frac{1}{n} B(e,n)$ converge, in the Hausdorff sense on the asymptotic cone, to a convex body invariant under the action of a stratified nilpotent Lie group, and we compute the resulting homogeneous dimension explicitly in terms of the lower central series of the associated nilshadow.

As applications, we derive an exact formula for the leading coefficient in the asymptotic expansion $V(n) = c \cdot n^d + o(n^d)$ in terms of the Haar measure on the nilpotent Lie group arising as the asymptotic cone, generalizing prior computations of Pansu and Breuillard for discrete finitely generated nilpotent groups to the locally compact setting. We further discuss the regularity of the growth function, proving that $V(n)/n^d$ converges, and give examples illustrating that the convergence rate can be arbitrarily slow, contrasting with the discrete case. Finally, we relate our results to the structure theory of amenable locally compact groups and discuss consequences for random walks and heat kernel estimates on such groups.

# Abstract

Pansu's foundational thesis established that Carnot–Carathéodory metrics on nilpotent Lie groups arise naturally as asymptotic cones of finitely generated nilpotent groups, providing a geometric framework linking discrete group theory to sub-Riemannian geometry. This work extends Pansu's construction to the broader setting of general locally compact groups of polynomial growth, encompassing both discrete and continuous cases within a unified structural theory.

We show that every locally compact group of polynomial growth admits an asymptotic cone that is well-defined up to bi-Lipschitz equivalence, and that this cone carries the structure of a locally compact, connected, locally connected metric space equipped with a transitive action by a nilpotent Lie group. Building on the Breuillard–Green–Tao/Losert structure theory for approximate groups and groups of polynomial growth, we establish that such groups admit a nested sequence of compact normal subgroups whose quotients are amenable and virtually nilpotent, allowing us to relate the asymptotic geometry directly to an associated graded nilpotent Lie group equipped with a canonically defined homogeneous quasi-metric.

As a consequence, we obtain a generalized Gromov-type theorem characterizing polynomial growth in terms of virtual nilpotency for locally compact compactly generated groups, extending the Milnor–Wolf and Gromov theorems beyond the discrete setting. We further establish a local limit theorem for random walks on such groups, showing that suitably normalized transition probabilities converge to a heat kernel on the limiting nilpotent Lie group, thereby extending results of Alexopoulos, Breuillard, and Diaconis–Hough. 

Applications to ergodic theory are developed through the study of pointwise ergodic theorems along subsequences and averaging sequences adapted to the polynomial volume growth structure. We show that Følner sequences arising from the metric balls of the asymptotic cone satisfy strong sweeping-out avoidance properties, yielding new pointwise ergodic theorems for actions of locally compact groups of polynomial growth on probability spaces. These results provide a geometric-analytic bridge between the coarse geometry of polynomial growth groups and the fine ergodic behavior of their measure-preserving actions, with applications to random walks on homogeneous spaces and to the study of unipotent flows arising from lattices in Lie groups of polynomial growth type.

We study the asymptotic behavior of volumes of balls in finitely generated groups of polynomial growth, with particular attention to the refined structure of the volume growth function beyond leading-order asymptotics. Building on Gromov's theorem and Breuillard–Green–Tao's structural results, we establish precise volume asymptotics for a broad class of nilpotent and virtually nilpotent groups, expressed in terms of explicit polynomial and logarithmic correction terms tied to the associated graded Lie algebra structure.

A central theme of this work is the phenomenon of weak commensurability between polynomial growth groups and solvable (in particular, nilpotent) Lie groups equipped with left-invariant Riemannian or sub-Riemannian metrics. We show that volume asymptotics are preserved under weak commensurability, allowing volume growth data on the discrete group side to be transferred to and computed via continuous Lie group models, and vice versa. This correspondence yields sharp volume comparison estimates and clarifies the extent to which asymptotic cone geometry determines finer volume statistics.

As an application, we resolve a question of Burago concerning the existence and characterization of exact volume growth asymptotics (rather than merely growth *rates*) for polynomial growth groups, showing that the second-order term in the volume expansion is governed by an explicit invariant of the associated nilpotent shadow. This provides a complete answer in the setting originally proposed by Burago and clarifies the boundary between rigidity phenomena dictated by the growth rate alone and finer geometric invariants visible only at the level of exact asymptotics.

Our methods combine tools from asymptotic cone theory, Lie group rescaling limits, and quantitative equidistribution techniques, and they suggest further applications to volume asymptotics in more general polynomial growth settings, including groups with torsion and non-discrete locally compact analogues.

# On the Asymptotic Geometry of Locally Compact Groups with Polynomial Growth

## Abstract

We investigate the large-scale geometric structure of locally compact, compactly generated groups of polynomial growth, focusing on the asymptotic shape of large balls with respect to a word (or gauge) metric associated to a compact generating set. Building on the Breuillard–Le Donne refinement of the Guivarc'h–Bass–Pansu theorem, we show that the sequence of rescaled balls $(B(n)/n)_{n \geq 1}$ converges, in the local Hausdorff sense, to a compact, symmetric, convex subset $K$ of the associated graded nilpotent Lie group equipped with its Carnot–Carathéodory (or a suitable homogeneous) metric. We give quantitative estimates for the rate of this convergence in terms of the structure constants of the underlying nilshadow and its associated stratified Lie algebra, extending previous results known in the discrete, finitely generated case to the locally compact setting.

A central motivation for this work comes from Stoll's striking discovery that the growth series of certain finitely generated nilpotent groups—specifically some quotients of the discrete Heisenberg-type groups—can fail to be rational functions, in contrast to the rationality established by Benson and Shapiro for groups of Heisenberg type and by others for various classes of nilpotent groups. We revisit Stoll's examples from the point of view of the limiting shape $K$: we show that the failure of rationality is intimately tied to irregularities and non-polytopal features in the asymptotic unit ball, and we relate the arithmetic of the growth series to the combinatorics of the faces of $K$. In particular, we show that when the limit shape $K$ is a rational polytope with respect to a natural lattice structure, the growth series exhibits the expected rational behavior, whereas curvature or transcendental features of $\partial K$ obstruct rationality, providing a geometric explanation for Stoll's phenomenon.

We further extend these considerations to the locally compact setting, where the relevant "growth series" is replaced by the asymptotic volume function $V(n) = \mu(B(n))$, and we establish polynomial asymptotic expansions
$$
V(n) = c_d n^d + c_{d-1} n^{d-1} + \cdots
$$
with coefficients expressed via the volume of $K$ and correction terms coming from the discrepancy between the word metric and its homogeneous approximation. These results unify and extend prior work of Pansu, Breuillard, Tessera, and Stoll, and clarify the extent to which rationality phenomena for growth series are special to the discrete setting versus reflecting more robust geometric features of the asymptotic cone.

# Abstract

We extend Pansu's classical results on the asymptotic geometry of nilpotent Lie groups to the setting of arbitrary locally compact, compactly generated groups. Given such a group $G$ equipped with a word metric associated to a compact generating set, we investigate the existence and structure of asymptotic cones and their relationship to Lie-theoretic approximations of $G$.

Central to our approach is the notion of a **Lie shadow**: a locally compact group $H$ (typically Lie, or an inverse limit of Lie groups) that captures the large-scale geometry of $G$ through a sequence of controlled approximations, generalizing the role played by the associated graded nilpotent Lie group in Pansu's theorem for Carnot groups. We show that under natural conditions—including polynomial growth or, more generally, the existence of a suitable contracting automorphism structure—the group $G$ admits a Lie shadow $H$ such that the rescaled Cayley graphs of $G$ converge in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to a geometric model built from $H$, equipped with a homogeneous quasi-metric.

A significant portion of the manuscript is devoted to quantifying the **speed of convergence** in this asymptotic limit. We establish explicit bounds, in terms of the word metric on $G$ and the algebraic data defining the shadow $H$, that measure the distortion between the rescaled metric on $G$ and the limiting metric on $H$ at scale $R$. These estimates refine and extend quantitative versions of Pansu's differentiability theorem for quasi-isometries, and they yield effective error terms that are polynomial (or, in favorable cases, exponential) in $1/R$, depending on the regularity of the contracting automorphism and the local structure of $G$ near the identity.

Finally, we present applications to **ergodic theory** on locally compact groups. Using the quantitative convergence results, we derive effective ergodic theorems for measure-preserving actions of $G$, extending the Pansu-type approach to non-nilpotent settings. In particular, we obtain rates of convergence for spherical and ball averages associated to word metrics, and we discuss consequences for the study of harmonic functions, random walks, and boundary theory on $G$. These results provide a unified geometric framework linking large-scale structure, Lie-theoretic approximation, and dynamical behavior for a broad class of locally compact groups.
